analysis.problem_summary: Determine if repeatedly replacing a positive integer with the sum of the squares of its digits eventually reaches 1 or falls into an infinite repeating loop.
analysis.intuition: When repeatedly calculating the sum of squares of digits, large numbers rapidly shrink (for example, the largest 32-bit integer produces a sum well under 250 in one step). Because the set of possible numbers in the sequence is small and bounded, the process will either reach 1 or cycle endlessly through previously visited numbers. Using a hash set to store each intermediate number allows us to detect when we have entered a loop.
approach: Define a helper function sumOfSquaresOfDigits(n) that extracts each digit using n % 10, squares it, adds it to a total sum, and reduces n using integer division n / 10 until n is 0.
Initialize a HashSet of integers named set to track numbers encountered in the chain.
Execute a while loop that runs as long as n is not equal to 1.
Inside the loop, check if set already contains n; if it does, a cycle is detected, so return false.
Add the current value of n to set to mark it as visited.
If the loop terminates because n becomes 1, return true.
analysis.why_it_works: The process is a deterministic state transition where each number maps to exactly one next number. Since the values quickly drop below 243 for any 32-bit integer, there are only finitely many distinct values the sequence can take. By Dirichlet's box principle (pigeonhole principle), the chain must either hit 1 (and stay there) or repeat a value. The hash set acts as a memory of visited states; returning false as soon as a duplicate number appears correctly identifies non-terminating infinite loops.
analysis.time_explanation: Computing the sum of squared digits takes O(log n) time based on the number of digits, and for values under 243, the chain length is bounded by a small constant.
analysis.space_explanation: The hash set stores at most O(log n) distinct numbers generated during the sequence before reaching 1 or entering a loop.
analysis.key_takeaway: When repeatedly applying a deterministic function generates a sequence of bounded values, a Hash Set can effectively detect infinite loops by identifying duplicate states.
